cse-1993-ii-a-6-5.approach: Convert the binary fraction by positional weights, and the decimal integer to hex by repeated division by 16.
pitfalls: Reading remainders top-down gives E54, which is wrong.

cse-1993-ii-a-6-6.approach: A ROM truth table has one word per input combination and one output bit per product bit.

steps.title: Words (address lines)
steps.body: Inputs = two 4-bit numbers = $8$ address bits, so $M = 2^8 = 256$ words.

steps.title: Bits per word
steps.body: Largest product: $15 \times 15 = 225 < 2^8 = 256$, so the product needs $4+4 = 8$ bits. $N = 8$.

pitfalls: Using 16 words (only 4 address bits) or 16 output bits.
cse-1993-ii-a-6-6.verification: $225 = (11100001)_2$ fits in 8 bits; $2^8$ combinations cover every operand pair.

cse-1993-ii-a-6-7.approach: Average rotational latency is half a revolution; one track passes under the head per revolution, so transfer rate = track capacity × revolutions per second.

steps.title: Revolution time
steps.body: $2400$ rpm $= 2400/60 = 40$ rev/s, so one revolution takes $1/40$ s $= 25$ ms.

steps.title: Average latency
steps.body: $P = \tfrac12 \times 25 = 12.5$ ms.

pitfalls: Taking a full revolution (25 ms) as the average latency.
The number of tracks (200) is irrelevant here.

cse-1993-ii-a-6-8.approach: In every 1 ms period the CPU loses only the save + service + restore time; the first 10 µs after arrival is still main-program execution.
cse-1993-ii-a-6-8.given:
| Phase | Time |
|---|---|
| Main program continues after arrival | 10 µs |
| Save CPU state | 10 µs |
| Interrupt service | 80 µs |
| Restore CPU state | 10 µs |
| Interrupt period | 1 ms = 1000 µs |

steps.title: Time lost per interrupt
steps.body: $10 + 80 + 10 = 100\ \mu s$ (the low part of the waveform).

pitfalls: Counting the 10 µs before the state is saved as overhead gives 89%, but the figure shows the main program still running then.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-1.approach: Both formals of P are var parameters bound to the same global m, so x := y+1 writes 0+1 into global m; P's local m is a different variable.

steps.title: Binding
steps.body: `P(m, m)`: `x` and `y` are both references (aliases) to the global `m`, which is $0$.

steps.title: Body of P
steps.body: `m := 1` sets P's **local** `m` only. `x := y + 1` reads global $m = 0$ through `y` and stores $1$ into global `m` through `x`.

steps.title: Output
steps.body: `write(m)` prints $1$.

answer.value: 1 — x and y are references to m, which P modifies

optionAnalysis.reason: The local m of P shadows the global and is a different variable; it is not what is printed.
y is 0 when read, but the assignment through x changes m to 1.
x and y alias m; x := y + 1 sets m to 1.

pitfalls: Thinking P's local m := 1 is the reason the output is 1.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-2.approach: n*1 is an expression passed by value to x, and n is passed by reference to y; Q only assigns to its local copy x, so n is unchanged.

steps.title: Binding
steps.body: `Q(n*1, n)`: `x` gets a copy of the value $0$; `y` is a reference to `n`.

steps.title: Body of Q
steps.body: `x := y + 1` writes $1$ into the local copy `x` only; `n` (through `y`) is only read.

steps.title: Output
steps.body: `write(n)` prints $0$.

answer.value: 0 — n is bound to y, which is only read

optionAnalysis.reason: n is not the actual parameter for x; the expression n*1 is.
n is bound to the var parameter y, which Q never assigns, so n stays 0.
Output is 0; y is only read.

pitfalls: Treating n*1 as a reference to n.
cse-1993-ii-a-7-2.verification: Only x (a value copy) is assigned in Q.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-3.approach: A global name is visible in every nested block except those that redeclare it; P declares its own m, Q does not.

steps.title: Where m is redeclared
steps.body: P has `var m : integer;`, so inside P the name `m` means P's local and the global `m` is hidden.

steps.title: Scope
steps.body: Q declares no `m`, so the global `m` is visible in the main program PARAM and in Q: scope = PARAM, Q.

optionAnalysis.reason: Inside P the global m is hidden by the local m.
Includes P (hidden there) and omits Q.
Visible in PARAM and Q, hidden in P.
Omits the main program and includes P.

pitfalls: Confusing aliasing (P can modify global m through x) with scope (the name m in P is the local one).
cse-1993-ii-a-7-3.verification: Name lookup in P finds P's own m first.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-4.approach: This is the classic swap without a temporary: trace with symbolic values a = A, b = B.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Now $a = B$, $b = A$: the values are exchanged (ignoring overflow).

optionAnalysis.reason: Trace gives a = B, b = A.

pitfalls: Overflow of a + b can break the swap on fixed-width integers, but that is not what is asked.
cse-1993-ii-a-7-4.verification: Example a=3, b=5: a=8, b=3, a=5.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-5.approach: After ptr := nil the next statement dereferences nil, which is detected only when the program runs.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: `new(ptr)` allocates a record; `ptr := nil` throws that address away (a memory leak).

steps.title: Dereference
steps.body: `ptr^.d := 5.2` accesses the record pointed to by `nil`. Type-checking passes (ptr^ is a data record and d is real), so the failure is a **run-time** error, specifically a nil-pointer dereference.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: (b) and (d) are true; 5.2 is never printed.

optionAnalysis.reason: The dereference is well-typed; nil-ness is only known at run time (see the pitfall about writeln).
The run-time error is exactly a nil pointer dereference.

pitfalls: Strictly, standard Pascal cannot write a pointer, so writeln(ptr) is a compile error; the intended point of the question is the nil dereference.
cse-1993-ii-a-7-5.verification: ptr is nil at the assignment, so ptr^ has no storage.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-6.approach: Pass 1 of a two-pass assembler only defines things (location counter, symbol and literal tables); pass 2 generates code.

steps.title: Pass 1
steps.body: Advances the location counter over every statement, enters labels with their addresses into the symbol table, collects literals and assigns them addresses (at LTORG/END), and ends knowing the program length.

steps.title: Pass 2
steps.body: Uses those tables to generate machine code for all instructions, including loads and stores.

optionAnalysis.reason: Literals are given addresses in pass 1.
The final location counter gives the program length.
Building the symbol table is the main job of pass 1.
Code is generated in pass 2, when forward references are known.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-6.verification: Forward references can only be resolved after pass 1, so code generation must be in pass 2.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-7.approach: The loader is what brings every other program into memory, so it must itself already be resident.

steps.title: Reason
steps.body: Editors, assemblers and linkers are ordinary programs that are loaded only when needed. Loading any of them requires the loader, so the loader (at least its bootstrap part) must always be in main memory.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Of the listed programs only the loader must always be resident.

optionAnalysis.reason: Linking can be done in advance; the linker is loaded on demand.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-7.verification: Without a resident loader no other program could be brought into memory.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-8.approach: The file system must find the root directory without any other directory, so it has to be at a known, fixed location on the disk.

steps.title: Reason
steps.body: Every path lookup starts at the root. Nothing points to the root, so its location must be fixed and known in advance on each disk (for example just after the boot block or superblock).

steps.title: Not main memory
steps.body: Main memory is volatile, so the root directory cannot live only there; and "anywhere" would make it impossible to find.

answer.value: at a fixed location on the disk

optionAnalysis.reason: Memory is volatile; the directory must be on disk.
A fixed location lets it be found without any lookup.
Every disk with a file system has its own root directory, not only the system disk.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-8.verification: Matches real layouts (e.g. the FAT root directory at a fixed sector after the FATs).

cse-1993-ii-a-7-9.approach: Worst case: each process holds one less than its peak; one extra unit then guarantees someone can finish.

steps.title: Worst case
steps.body: Maximum held without anyone finishing: $(3-1)+(4-1)+(6-1) = 2+3+5 = 10$.

steps.title: Condition
steps.body: Deadlock is impossible iff $m \ge 10 + 1 = 11$.

steps.title: Options
steps.body: $7, 9, 10 < 11$ (deadlock possible); $13, 15 \ge 11$ (deadlock-free).

optionAnalysis.reason: 7 < 11: e.g. A holds 2, B 3, C 2, all waiting.
With 10, holdings 2, 3, 5 leave none free: deadlock.

pitfalls: Choosing 10 — the sum of (need − 1) still deadlocks; one more is required.
cse-1993-ii-a-7-9.verification: With 11, holdings 2+3+5 leave 1 free, enough for some process to reach its peak.

cse-1993-ii-a-7-10.approach: Simulate round robin with quantum 1 from the ready order p, q, r, s, t.

steps.title: Round 1
steps.body: 0–1 p (3 left), 1–2 q (done at 2), 2–3 r (7 left), 3–4 s (done at 4), 4–5 t (1 left).

scene.caption: q and s finish in the first round

steps.title: Round 2
steps.body: Queue: p, r, t. 5–6 p (2 left), 6–7 r (6 left), 7–8 t (done at 8).

steps.title: Round 3
steps.body: Queue: p, r. 8–9 p (1 left), 9–10 r (5 left), 10–11 p (done at **11**).

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Only r remains and runs 11–16. Completion time of p = $11$.

optionAnalysis.reason: 4 is p's burst, its finish time under FCFS.
At 10 p still has 1 unit left (r ran 9–10).

cse-1993-ii-a-7-10.shortcut: Up to p's last slice the CPU runs p 4 times, q and s once, t twice and r 3 times: 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 11.
cse-1993-ii-a-7-10.verification: Total burst 16 = r's finish time, consistent with the schedule.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-1.approach: A connected graph with n vertices needs n−1 edges to be a tree; one extra edge creates exactly one cycle.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Connected with $n$ edges $= (n-1)+1$: a spanning tree plus one edge, so $G$ has **exactly one** cycle.

steps.title: Removing edges
steps.body: Removing a cycle edge leaves a connected tree, so (b) fails. Removing any two edges leaves $n-2 < n-1$ edges, which can never connect $n$ vertices, so (d) holds.

optionAnalysis.reason: n edges on n connected vertices force a cycle.
Removing an edge on the cycle keeps G connected.
n − 2 edges cannot connect n vertices.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-1.verification: Example: cycle $C_4$ (4 vertices, 4 edges): has a cycle, stays connected after removing one edge, disconnected after removing two.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-2.approach: Distribute ∧ over ∨ and drop the contradiction.

steps.title: Distribute
steps.body: $p \wedge (\sim p \vee q) \equiv (p \wedge \sim p) \vee (p \wedge q)$.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.body: $p \wedge \sim p \equiv F$, so the expression is $F \vee (p \wedge q) \equiv p \wedge q$.

optionAnalysis.reason: p = F, q = T makes p ∨ q true but the proposition false.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-2.verification: Truth table: only p = T, q = T makes it true, same as p ∧ q.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-3.approach: A finite union of finite sets is finite, so an infinite set split into finitely many pieces must have an infinite piece.

steps.title: Contrapositive
steps.body: If every $S_i$ were finite, $|S| \le |S_1| + \dots + |S_n|$ would be finite — contradiction. So at least one $S_i$ is infinite.

steps.title: Other options
steps.body: Take $S = \mathbb N$, $n = 2$, $S_1 = S_2 = \mathbb N$: no $S_i$ is finite and two are infinite, refuting (a) and (d). Take $S_1 = \{1\}, S_2 = \{2\}, S_3 = \mathbb N$: two finite sets, refuting (b).

answer.value: at least one S_i is infinite

cse-1993-ii-a-8-3.verification: Counter-examples given for every other option.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-4.approach: |A × A| = n², and a set of size k has 2^k subsets.

steps.title: Size of A × A
steps.body: $|A\times A| = n \cdot n = n^2$.

steps.title: Power set
steps.body: $|\mathcal P(A\times A)| = 2^{n^2}$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $2^{2^n}$ is the size of the power set of the power set of A.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-5.approach: A partial order must be reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; < is irreflexive, so it fails — then check each option's stated reason.

steps.title: Properties of <
steps.body: Irreflexive ($a<a$ never holds), asymmetric (hence also antisymmetric), transitive.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body: Not reflexive ⇒ **not** a partial order (it is a strict order).

steps.title: Reasons in the options
steps.body: (a), (b) wrongly call it a partial order. (c) says it is not asymmetric — false. (d) says it is not antisymmetric — false. So no option gives a correct reason: (e).

optionAnalysis.reason: < is not reflexive, so not a partial order.
< is asymmetric, so the reason is false.
< is antisymmetric (vacuously), so "not antisymmetric" is false; read as "not (antisymmetric and reflexive)" it would be acceptable.
No option gives both a correct verdict and a correct reason.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-5.verification: 1 < 1 is false, so reflexivity fails; the other two properties hold.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-6.approach: Map the m elements of A one by one to distinct elements of B.

steps.title: Choices
steps.body: First element: $n$ choices, second $n-1$, …, $m$-th $n-m+1$.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $n(n-1)\cdots(n-m+1) = \dfrac{n!}{(n-m)!} = {}^nP_m$.

optionAnalysis.reason: $m^n$ counts all functions from B to A.
${}^nC_m$ only chooses the image set; it ignores the m! orderings.

cse-1993-ii-a-8-7.approach: n terms, each at most c·n, sum to at most c·n²; constant factors inside O do not matter.

steps.title: Bound
steps.body: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} O(n) \le \sum_{k=1}^{n} c\,n = c\,n^2$, so the sum is $O(n^2)$.

steps.title: Equivalent forms
steps.body: $O(3n^2) = O(1.5n^2) = O(n^2)$, and every $O(n^2)$ function is also $O(n^3)$ (a valid, loose upper bound). It is not $O(n)$ in general.

optionAnalysis.reason: n terms of size ~n give ~n², not O(n).
Valid (loose) upper bound since n² ≤ n³.

pitfalls: If only tight bounds are wanted, (c) would be excluded; big-O is an upper bound, so it is formally correct.
cse-1993-ii-a-8-7.verification: Each term = n gives exactly n², which is in every class (b)–(e) but not O(n).
